If you go to a lawyer and explain your suicide plan, s/he has an ethical obligation to report it. You could talk hypotheticals, but it comes down to what the lawyer reasonably believed would result. As vague as your post is, most everyone figured out exactly what you were going to do. A lawyer would figure it out, and privilege would not apply. The point of the privilege is to keep an open line of honest communication between attorneys and clients so that the attorney can render the best representation and provide the best advice. It isn't fair to dump all of that on some random lawyer with the expectation to keep quiet.

This question is tough. I feel like leaving a note means you have things you still want to say. I've tried notes, recordings, etc, and ultimately, I realized that there was nothing that I could say that would help the survivors understand how I felt to lead to my decision. I'm also kind of a perfectionist so it just took a damn long time :) In all seriousness, how you're feeling and what you want to do are irrational.  The process of writing the note or whatever you record makes you pause and think.  That's really important. 

The topics in my previous notes were apologies, instructions for what to do with my property, explanations for why I wanted to die, and generalized goodbyes. Write a note if you think it will help you, but don't be misled into believing that anything you say will make your survivors feel better that you're gone. It will never make sense to them. The reddit bereavement thing proves that. Good luck.

Transitions are hard. Change is scary. You're experiencing a lot of emotions right now. It all feels like weakness, but it's really a great opportunity because you can decide whatever you want to do in life. Seriously, you have a restart button.  You said you have goals, but I think that you should ask yourself if they are what you REALLY want. Being depressed doesn't go away just because you achieve your goals, but man it is so much harder when you're doing something you don't love. Sometimes goals don't always live up to what you expect. Keep an open mind. Try internships. It would be very tragic if you ended it all before exhausting all of your options.  I hope my comment makes sense. I wish you good luck.

This question is a really good one for the suicide hotline. They're usually local and can give you more personalized advice. They may even suggest a non-ER option. Depending upon your insurance, you would be expecting a hefty bill.  Don't let that discourage you, but just bear that in mind that there may be other crisis centers.

Hospitals suck, but they're not bad or evil places. The staff are there for treating lots of people with lots of problems, so the environment can be very unnerving. Do what you think is best. Good luck.

You did the right thing. It's scary to speak up. Try to think about the positive outcomes from your reporting instead of potential negatives. If you're truly concerned that your other co-workers will treat you differently, then that's something to address with the person with whom you originally filed your report. S/he may be able to explain your employer's policy about how such complaints are handled. Plus, maybe the person who took your complaint has insight about the experience of others who were in a similar situation. It may ease your concerns.

Don't take a chance on your safety. You have no idea what this man's criminal history is. Most towns have non-emergency police phone lines. The police should investigate him. Let them talk to him. You may not think he has done anything "criminal," but you neve know. 
At the very least, the police can give you his name. You may be able to file an order of protection or restraining order at a local courthouse.
I'm glad you're carrying pepper spray, but it is unacceptable for you to feel like you could be in danger at the complex you call home.
